questions.question: A Markov Decision Process (MDP) formalizes a reinforcement learning problem. Which of the following are components of an MDP?

options.text: A set of states S that the agent can occupy
A set of actions A available in each state
A transition function T(s, a, s') giving the probability of reaching s' from s after action a
A reward function R(s, a) giving the expected immediate reward
A labeled training set of (input, output) pairs

questions.explanation: An MDP is the tuple (S, A, T, R) plus a discount factor γ. There are no labeled (input, output) pairs in RL — that is supervised learning. The agent learns from the scalar reward signal, which is indirect and potentially delayed. (a) is too strong: MDPs assume the state is a sufficient statistic but real-world agents often deal with partial observability (POMDPs). The strict guarantee of 'fully observable at all times' is not part of the formal definition.

questions.question: Consider the experience tuple (s, a, s', r) used in reinforcement learning. Which statements about it are correct?

options.text: It captures one atomic learning event: the agent was in state s, took action a, landed in s', and received reward r
It provides the minimum information needed for one Q-learning update
The next state s' is always deterministically determined by (s, a)
The reward r may be zero for most tuples in environments with delayed reward
Experience tuples can be stored and replayed to improve sample efficiency

questions.explanation: Experience tuples are the atomic learning unit. In stochastic environments, (s, a) induces a probability distribution over s' — it is not deterministic in general. Delayed rewards mean many tuples will have r=0 until a terminal event. Storing tuples enables experience replay. (b) is wrong — a single tuple updates Q at one point; discovering the optimal policy requires exploration across the entire state-action space.

questions.question: Concerning the discount factor γ in the discounted cumulative reward Σ γ^(i-1) · r_i, which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Setting γ near 0 produces a myopic agent that prioritizes immediate rewards
Setting γ near 1 makes the agent value distant future rewards almost as much as immediate ones
γ > 1 is commonly used to boost the importance of long-term rewards
A smaller γ can make the infinite-horizon sum converge more easily
γ = 0 makes the agent completely ignore the reward signal

questions.explanation: γ ∈ [0, 1). Values > 1 are not used because they would cause the infinite sum to diverge. γ = 0 does NOT ignore rewards — it still values the immediate reward r_1 (since γ^0 = 1), but zeros every future term. Smaller γ accelerates convergence of the infinite-horizon sum.

questions.question: You are asked to distinguish between model-based and model-free reinforcement learning. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Model-based RL explicitly constructs or is given the transition function T and reward function R, then applies dynamic programming
Model-free RL derives a policy from sampled experience without explicitly learning T or R
Q-learning is a model-free algorithm
Policy iteration and value iteration are model-based algorithms
Model-free methods always converge faster than model-based methods when the model is known exactly

questions.explanation: Model-based uses T and R (e.g., policy/value iteration); model-free (e.g., Q-learning) learns Q directly from samples. When a perfect model is available, model-based methods like value iteration converge dramatically faster than model-free sampling methods because they can sweep the entire state space at each step. (b) is wrong: model-free RL still knows the state and action spaces — it just doesn't learn T or R explicitly.

questions.question: Consider the Bellman optimality equation: V*(s) = max_a [ R(s, a) + γ · Σ_{s'} T(s, a, s') · V*(s') ]. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: V*(s) is defined only for deterministic environments and is undefined under stochastic transitions
The equation is not recursive; each V*(s) is computed independently
The max operator captures the assumption that the agent will act optimally from state s onward
Value iteration solves this equation by iteratively applying the right-hand side until convergence
The equation only holds for deterministic environments

questions.explanation: The Bellman equation is the foundation of DP-based RL. It is general — the summation Σ_{s'} T(s, a, s') · V*(s') handles stochastic transitions; for deterministic environments, T becomes an indicator function and the sum collapses to a single term. (a) is false — V* is well-defined for stochastic MDPs via the expectation. (b) is false — the Bellman equation IS recursive.

questions.question: An RL policy π maps states to actions. Which of the following statements about policies are correct?

options.text: A policy π always maps each state to a SET of actions with equal probability
A stochastic policy is mathematically impossible in discrete MDPs
A stochastic policy produces a probability distribution over actions per state
Every state must map to a unique optimal action — ties are disallowed
An ε-greedy policy is purely exploratory

questions.explanation: Ties are allowed — any action attaining the max is optimal. ε-greedy is a MIX: greedy (exploitation) with probability 1−ε and random (exploration) with probability ε; it is not purely exploratory. (a) is false — a policy can be deterministic (single action) or stochastic. (b) is false — stochastic policies are standard.

questions.question: Regarding finite-horizon vs. infinite-horizon problem formulations in RL, which statements are correct?

options.text: Finite-horizon and infinite-horizon problems always yield identical optimal policies
Discounting is NEVER used in finite-horizon problems
A finite-horizon problem always yields a different optimal policy than an infinite-horizon version of the same environment
Discounting is commonly used to make infinite-horizon returns mathematically well-defined
An infinite-horizon undiscounted problem is always solvable by standard value iteration

questions.explanation: Finite-horizon policies can be non-stationary (depend on time remaining). Infinite-horizon with γ<1 yields stationary policies. The two formulations MAY produce the same policy for some problems. Undiscounted infinite-horizon can have unbounded value — not always solvable by standard VI. (a) is false — finite-horizon policies can depend on time remaining. (b) is false — discounting is orthogonal to horizon and often applied to both.

questions.question: Which of the following are important distinctions between reinforcement learning and supervised learning?

options.text: Supervised learning provides (input, target) labels; RL provides only a scalar reward signal
RL has delayed, scalar rewards whereas supervised learning has immediate labeled targets
Supervised learning typically has i.i.d. training samples; RL samples are sequentially dependent via the environment
RL requires exploration to discover which actions yield rewards; supervised learning does not
RL is a special case of unsupervised learning because there are no target labels

questions.explanation: RL is NOT a special case of unsupervised learning: the reward signal is a form of supervised feedback, just sparse and delayed. Options (a)–(d) are the canonical distinctions. (b) is false — RL receives a scalar reward, not action labels. That's precisely what distinguishes it from imitation learning.

questions.question: Consider the credit assignment problem in RL. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: It asks how to distribute a delayed reward back to the earlier actions that produced it
Discounting with γ < 1 assigns exponentially smaller credit to rewards further in the future
The temporal-difference target r + γ · max_{a'} Q(s', a') implicitly back-propagates future value estimates through time
Credit assignment is trivial when rewards are received at every time step
Eligibility traces are one solution that remembers which states/actions were recently visited

questions.explanation: Credit assignment is non-trivial even with dense rewards: rewards received now may be the result of long chains of decisions, and disentangling which past action mattered is still hard. (d) is too strong. (b) is wrong — γ > 1 is not used (divergence). Discounting with γ < 1 lets earlier actions receive credit via γ^k attenuation.

questions.question: The 'sense-think-act' cycle describes the basic loop of a reinforcement-learning agent. Which of the following are part of this loop?

options.text: Sense: observe the current state s of the environment
Think: consult the current policy π to select an action given the current state
Act: execute a in the environment, producing s' and reward r
Learn: update internal estimates (Q-values, policy, or model) based on (s, a, s', r)
Forget: flush all prior experience before the next iteration

questions.explanation: Sense-think-act-learn is the full loop. Forgetting prior experience would prevent learning; experience replay and persistent Q-tables are how agents ACCUMULATE knowledge over time. (b) describes pure random behavior, not the 'think' step — which is policy evaluation.

questions.question: Given the Q-learning update rule Q'[s, a] = (1 − α) · Q[s, a] + α · (r + γ · max_{a'} Q[s', a']), which of the following statements are TRUE?

options.text: α is the learning rate controlling how much a new estimate overrides the existing Q-value
γ is the discount factor controlling the relative weight of future vs. immediate rewards
The target value is r + γ · max_{a'} Q[s', a'] — what Q[s, a] is being pulled toward
Setting α = 1 makes Q[s, a] equal to the one-sample target and discards all prior learning
The max over a' means Q-learning is on-policy

questions.explanation: Options (a)–(d) describe the update mechanics correctly. (e) is FALSE — the max operator is OFF-policy: it uses the greedy policy in the target regardless of which policy (e.g., ε-greedy) generated the experience. This is precisely what makes Q-learning off-policy. (b) confuses γ with ε. γ is the discount factor; ε is the exploration rate in ε-greedy.

questions.question: Why is Q-learning called an 'off-policy' algorithm?

options.text: It can learn the optimal Q-function while following a different (exploratory) behavior policy
The target uses max_{a'} Q[s', a'] — the greedy action — not the action the behavior policy will actually take next
Off-policy means the algorithm updates happen on a different physical machine than the agent
Off-policy learning is impossible under function approximation in all settings
Off-policy means the algorithm cannot exploit learned Q-values during training

questions.explanation: The defining feature of off-policy learning: the update target is decoupled from the behavior policy. (c) is wrong — there IS a behavior policy (usually ε-greedy). (e) is wrong — exploitation happens; off-policy does NOT mean no exploitation. (c) is a distractor — 'off-policy' refers to learning-target independence from behavior policy, not hardware. (d) is false — off-policy with function approx is challenging but widely used (e.g., DQN).

questions.question: Regarding the exploration-exploitation tradeoff in Q-learning, which statements are correct?

options.text: Pure exploitation early in training can lock the agent into a suboptimal policy by never trying alternatives
Pure exploration never improves performance because the agent never acts greedily on what it has learned
ε-greedy with decaying ε is a standard schedule: high exploration early, high exploitation later
A small constant ε (e.g., 0.01) can suffice for stationary environments but fails when the environment changes
Q-learning converges to the optimal policy only if every state-action pair is visited infinitely often

questions.explanation: (b) is false — pure exploration yields unbiased Q estimates but zero practical performance; yet even pure exploration, with enough samples, produces a correct Q-table that can then be exploited. The statement 'never improves' overstates the effect. The other options are standard results (e) is a formal convergence condition. (a) is wrong — pure exploitation early on biases toward the first action that appears good and may miss better alternatives.

questions.question: Consider tuning the learning rate α in tabular Q-learning. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: A very large α (close to 1) can cause Q-values to oscillate in stochastic environments
A very small α makes learning stable but extremely slow
In stationary, deterministic environments, α = 1 is optimal because there is no noise to average out
Decaying α over time is a standard convergence trick
α must always equal γ to guarantee convergence

questions.explanation: α and γ serve completely different roles and need not be equal. In deterministic environments, α = 1 instantly replaces the old estimate with the new target, which is correct because there is no noise. In stochastic environments α < 1 is needed to average out randomness. (a) is wrong — large α causes oscillation in stochastic environments and prevents convergence.

questions.question: You observe a state transition (s, a, s', r) in Q-learning with α = 0.2, γ = 0.9. Suppose Q[s, a] = 5.0, and max_{a'} Q[s', a'] = 10.0, and r = 1. What are the correct statements about the Q update?

options.text: The target is r + γ · max_{a'} Q[s', a'] = 1 + 0.9 · 10 = 10
The updated Q[s, a] = 5 + 0.2 · (10 − 5) = 6.0 (the equivalent TD-error form)
If α were 1.0, Q[s, a] would stay at its original value of 5 because the update term vanishes
If γ were 0, Q[s, a] would immediately jump to 1

questions.explanation: Arithmetic (a)-(c) is correct. With α=1, Q is fully replaced with the target. (e) is wrong: with γ=0 the target is r=1 but the update is still (1−α)·5 + α·1 = 0.8·5+0.2·1 = 4.2, not 1. The target is 1, but α controls how much we move toward it. (d) is wrong — with α=1 the update fully replaces Q[s,a] with the target, not zeros the update.

questions.question: The temporal-difference (TD) error δ = r + γ · max_{a'} Q[s', a'] − Q[s, a] is central to Q-learning. Which statements about it are correct?

options.text: δ measures the discrepancy between the current Q estimate and the bootstrapped target
A large positive δ means the observed outcome was better than expected
A large negative δ means the observed outcome was worse than expected
Training aims to drive δ to zero across all visited (s, a) pairs
δ = 0 at every (s, a) pair implies Q equals the optimal Q*, regardless of which policy generated the data

questions.explanation: (e) is too strong — δ = 0 under the BEHAVIOR policy's visit distribution means Q is fixed point of the Bellman operator under that policy's support, but if the behavior policy does not explore all (s, a) pairs, Q may not equal Q* on unexplored pairs. (a) is false — δ can be negative when the realized outcome was worse than expected.

questions.question: For Q-learning to use a tabular Q-table on a trading problem with continuous features (e.g., Bollinger Band values), discretization is required. Which statements about discretization are correct?

options.text: Continuous values can be mapped to discrete buckets (e.g., 0–9) using percentiles of historical data
Too few buckets lose resolution; too many buckets inflate the state space and slow learning
Equal-width buckets may leave dense regions underrepresented; equal-frequency (percentile) buckets balance data per bucket
Discretization is unnecessary if the state space is continuous but the action space is discrete
A discretized state representation can harm performance if important distinctions fall within a single bucket

questions.explanation: Discrete actions don't make continuous states compatible with a tabular Q; tabular requires discrete states regardless of action space. Function approximation (e.g., NNs) handles continuous states natively. (a) overstates — discretization is standard when using a tabular Q-table.

questions.question: Which of the following are sufficient conditions for tabular Q-learning to converge to Q* with probability 1?

options.text: Every state-action pair must be visited infinitely often
The learning rate α_t must satisfy Σ α_t = ∞ and Σ α_t² < ∞
The environment must be a finite, stationary MDP
The initial Q-table must be initialized to all zeros
γ must be strictly less than 1 for infinite-horizon problems

questions.explanation: Initial values don't matter for convergence — any finite initialization converges under (a)–(c) and (e). The Robbins–Monro conditions on α_t ensure the stochastic approximation converges. (a) is wrong — the standard condition is 'visited infinitely often', not 'exactly once'.

questions.question: You initialize a Q-table optimistically (all Q-values set to an upper-bound estimate). What are the likely effects?

options.text: Optimistic initialization encourages the agent to try every action at least once because each starts with an inflated estimate
Optimistic initialization can partially substitute for explicit ε-greedy exploration early in training
Convergence may be slower than with a well-calibrated initialization, because the agent must 'correct' over-optimistic estimates
Optimistic initialization violates the convergence guarantees of Q-learning
This technique is most useful in stationary environments where Q-values decrease monotonically as data arrives

questions.explanation: Optimistic initialization is a valid exploration strategy and does NOT break convergence — any finite initialization converges under standard conditions. In non-stationary environments, the correction pattern is less predictable. (a) overstates — it encourages exploration but does not remove the need for many episodes.

questions.question: Suppose you replace the tabular Q with a neural network Q(s, a; θ). Which statements about function-approximation Q-learning are TRUE?

options.text: It can scale to continuous or very large state spaces where a table would be infeasible
It generalizes across similar states — updates to one state can affect Q-values of nearby states
Tabular Q-learning's convergence guarantees transfer without modification to neural-network Q approximation
Techniques like experience replay and target networks (DQN) help stabilize training
Function approximation eliminates the exploration/exploitation tradeoff

questions.explanation: Convergence guarantees for tabular Q-learning do NOT transfer to non-linear function approximation (the deadly triad: bootstrapping + off-policy + function approximation can diverge). Exploration is still needed. DQN's innovations address the stability issues. (c) is false — the 'deadly triad' (bootstrap + off-policy + function approx) can diverge without DQN-like fixes. (e) is false — exploration is still essential.

questions.question: Dyna-Q augments Q-learning with model-based planning. Which of the following correctly describe the Dyna-Q algorithm?

options.text: After each real experience (s, a, s', r), Dyna-Q updates BOTH the Q-table AND the model
It then performs many 'hallucinated' Q-updates using simulated experiences drawn from the learned model
Hallucinated experiences can be drawn from any state-action pair, including those never visited
Typical implementations perform 100–200 hallucinations per real experience
This dramatically accelerates convergence in environments where real experience is expensive

questions.explanation: Dyna-Q restricts hallucinations to previously visited (s, a) pairs — otherwise the model has no information to simulate from, and you'd 'drift into the abyss' with uninformed fabrications. (a) is wrong — Dyna-Q updates BOTH the Q-table AND the model on each real experience.

questions.question: Dyna-Q maintains an empirical transition-count table T_c and derives T[s, a, s'] from it. Which statements are correct?

options.text: T[s, a, s'] = T_c[s, a, s'] / Σ_{s''} T_c[s, a, s''] — normalize counts over possible next states
The learned model becomes more accurate as more real transitions are observed
Reward estimates are updated incrementally: R'[s, a] = (1 − α_R) · R[s, a] + α_R · r
The model must be initialized from a prior dataset — empirical counts cannot start at zero
Model accuracy directly limits the quality of hallucinated experiences

questions.explanation: (d) is wrong: empirical counts can start at zero; the agent simply won't hallucinate any (s, a) it hasn't experienced yet. The model is built purely from observed data. (b) is wrong — the model improves continuously as more real data arrives.

questions.question: Which of the following best describe why Dyna-Q accelerates learning relative to plain Q-learning?

options.text: Each real experience performs exactly one Q update and that is the ONLY update per real step
Dyna-Q requires more real experiences than Q-learning to converge
Hallucinations require no environmental interaction, so they are computationally much cheaper than real experiences
It fundamentally changes the convergence target of Q-learning
It removes the need for exploration

questions.explanation: Dyna-Q converges to the same Q* as plain Q-learning — it just uses data more efficiently. It does not remove the need for exploration: new (s, a) pairs must still be discovered through real interaction. (a) is false — Dyna-Q adds N hallucinated updates per real step. (b) is false — Dyna-Q uses each real experience MORE efficiently.

questions.question: Which of the following are genuine limitations or risks of Dyna-Q?

options.text: In non-stationary environments, the learned T and R become stale and hallucinations propagate obsolete information
In very high-dimensional state spaces, maintaining a count-based model T_c becomes infeasible
Poor exploration leads to a poor model, which leads to misleading hallucinations
Each hallucination requires a real environment call, so the cost savings are illusory
Hallucinations cannot teach the agent anything it could not have learned from its real experiences given infinite time

questions.explanation: (d) is the exact opposite of reality — hallucinations are purely in-memory and require NO real environment interaction, which is the whole point. (e) is true philosophically: hallucinations don't add new info, they just reuse existing info more efficiently. (a) is wrong — non-stationarity makes the learned model stale and hallucinations misleading.

questions.question: Consider a Dyna-Q agent with a stochastic environment. Which of the following are true about the hallucination step?

options.text: The next state s' is sampled from T[s, a, ·], not chosen deterministically
The reward is sampled from (or estimated by) R[s, a]
Hallucinated transitions can trigger new Q-value updates that propagate value backward along previously experienced trajectories
A very accurate model guarantees that Dyna-Q always outperforms plain Q-learning regardless of hallucination count
Zero hallucinations per real step reduces Dyna-Q to plain Q-learning

questions.explanation: (d) overstates — Dyna-Q cost scales with N hallucinations per step. Too many hallucinations on a small model can be wasteful. 0 hallucinations = plain Q-learning is the exact limiting case. (a) is wrong — s' is SAMPLED from T[s,a,·], not deterministically set to the mode.

questions.question: Which statement(s) correctly describe the relationship between Q-learning, Dyna-Q, and Dynamic Programming?

options.text: Dynamic Programming assumes a known model and performs exhaustive sweeps over the state space
Q-learning is purely model-free — it samples real experience and never builds a model
Dyna-Q is a hybrid — it samples real experience AND builds a model to enable planning via simulated experience
Dyna-Q is strictly faster than dynamic programming in problems where the true model is known and fits in memory
All three approaches can converge to the same optimal Q-function

questions.explanation: When the true model is known, DP sweeps are typically faster than Dyna-Q's sampled updates — Dyna-Q's advantage shines when the model must be LEARNED from samples. (a) is wrong — DP ASSUMES T and R are known; that is its defining feature.

questions.question: You are designing an RL trading agent. Which of the following are reasonable components of the agent's STATE representation?

options.text: The current Bollinger Band %B value for the traded stock
A flag indicating whether the agent is currently long, short, or flat
The realized return since entering the current position
The current portfolio cash balance
The action the agent WILL take next

questions.explanation: The action to be taken next is the OUTPUT of the policy, not the state. States are observations available at decision time. The others are all valid state components — indicators, position, and account-level info. (a) is not a useful state feature — it leaks implementation detail, not market information.

questions.question: Regarding reward design in an RL trading agent, which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Rewarding with daily return-per-share-held typically converges faster than rewarding only at exit
A 'reward only on exit' scheme imposes a harder credit-assignment problem because intermediate actions receive no feedback
Risk-adjusted rewards (e.g., incremental Sharpe contribution) discourage the agent from pursuing high-volatility bets
A poorly-designed reward can cause the agent to learn exploits (e.g., trade for commission rebates instead of profit)
Any monotonically increasing function of P&L produces the same optimal policy

questions.explanation: (e) is false — non-linear transforms change relative reward magnitudes and therefore the optimal trade-off between large and small gains, even if rankings are preserved. This matters because the Q-update is linear in reward. (a) is wrong — the opposite is true: delayed-only reward makes credit assignment harder and slows convergence.

questions.question: When training an RL trading agent, which of the following are best practices?

options.text: Train on an earlier time range and test on a later, strictly-subsequent time range
Re-train the agent multiple times on the same test set to find the best-performing run
Include realistic transaction costs (commission + market impact) during training so the policy learns to account for them
Use an adequate number of training iterations / episodes to allow Q-values to converge before evaluating
Discretize continuous indicators into a fixed, reasonably-sized bucket scheme if using a tabular Q-table

questions.explanation: (b) is implicit overfitting to the test set — a cardinal sin. Each re-selection based on test performance leaks test information into the model. (a) is wrong — random shuffling violates temporal causality and creates data leakage.

questions.question: Consider an RL agent trained on {BUY, SELL, HOLD} actions. Which statements are correct?

options.text: The 'holding' component of the state matters because legal actions depend on current position
Even if the policy receives the same indicator values on two different days, the optimal action can differ if the holding state differs
The agent can learn to trade only on directional predictions; risk management emerges automatically from Q-values
Over-trading (excessive BUY/SELL flipping) can be mitigated by including transaction costs in the reward
Reward shaping with a penalty for holding a losing position can encourage cutting losses faster

questions.explanation: (c) is false — proper risk management requires either explicit risk-penalized rewards or state features capturing risk; it does NOT emerge automatically from pure P&L maximization. (a) is wrong — holding state matters because the legal action set and risk depend on it.

questions.question: Which of the following are potential PITFALLS of applying Q-learning directly to financial markets?

options.text: Market non-stationarity invalidates learned Q-values over time
Low signal-to-noise ratio — a good policy is hard to distinguish from a lucky one
Limited training data — decades of daily bars may still be a tiny sample by ML standards
Backtesting look-ahead bias when state features encode information not actually available at decision time
Markets are perfectly stationary, so policies trained on 2005 data transfer directly to 2024 data

questions.explanation: (e) is the opposite of reality — market non-stationarity is one of the core challenges of applying RL to finance. (a) is wrong — markets have notoriously LOW signal-to-noise ratios.

questions.question: A trading agent's Q-table has converged. Which of the following are correct ways to USE it in production?

options.text: At each timestep, the action is always a uniformly random choice rather than argmax Q
Continuing to update Q in production is ALWAYS destructive and should be avoided
Freeze the Q-table permanently to avoid drift, even if the market regime changes
Maintain a small fraction of exploration (e.g., ε = 0.02) to continue discovering new states
If a state is observed that was never seen during training, the agent is guaranteed to make a sensible decision via the Q-table

questions.explanation: (c) is a reasonable strategy in some contexts but rigid — it fails in non-stationary markets. (e) is false: for unseen states, tabular Q returns its initial/default values, which may be meaningless. Function approximation is needed to generalize. (a) is false — in production we exploit the learned Q-table. (b) is false — small-α online updates help adapt to mild regime drift.

questions.question: The Efficient Markets Hypothesis (EMH) has three forms. Which of the following statements correctly characterize the WEAK form?

options.text: Current prices reflect all information contained in past prices and volumes
Technical analysis based on historical price patterns should not produce excess returns
Fundamental analysis is also ineffective
Insider trading cannot generate excess returns
It is the most restrictive form of the hypothesis

questions.explanation: Weak form: only historical prices are fully reflected. Fundamental analysis and insider information could still generate excess returns under weak form. Weak form is the LEAST restrictive, not the most.

questions.question: The SEMI-STRONG form of EMH asserts that prices reflect all public information. Which of the following are TRUE under this form?

options.text: Technical analysis cannot produce excess returns under semi-strong EMH
Fundamental analysis of public financial statements cannot produce excess returns
Private (insider) information could theoretically still produce excess returns
Exogenous public news (e.g., an oil-price shock) is also impounded in prices immediately
Managed mutual funds consistently beating their benchmarks is trivially consistent with semi-strong EMH

questions.explanation: (e) is false — consistent outperformance net of fees would be evidence AGAINST semi-strong EMH. However, SINGLE cases of outperformance can be consistent with semi-strong via survivorship/luck; consistent collective outperformance is harder to reconcile. (a) is wrong — TA uses past prices, which are public, so semi-strong EMH predicts TA fails.

questions.question: Consider evidence cited against the Efficient Markets Hypothesis. Which of the following are genuinely problematic for the hypothesis in its STRONG form?

options.text: Insider trading has never been documented empirically — it exists only in theory
Well-documented P/E ratio anomalies — low-P/E portfolios outperforming over 20-year horizons
The existence of Warren Buffett's long-term outperformance
Markets being open only during business hours
Hedge funds earning consistent alpha over decades

questions.explanation: Trading hours have nothing to do with market efficiency claims. The other options each challenge strong-form in different ways (insider edges, anomalies, persistent outperformance, alpha generation). Strong form is the most often rejected in practice. (a) is wrong — there are many documented insider-trading cases with clear evidence of excess returns.

questions.question: Romero & Balch's mining-company example illustrates the speed of price adjustment. A company reports lower-than-expected gold yield. Which effects on the stock price are consistent with semi-strong EMH?

options.text: The stock price adjusts over many quarters as retail investors digest the news
Prices remain unchanged until the next formal earnings release
The adjustment happens over many weeks as the information slowly disseminates to retail investors
Informed investors selling quickly to realize the loss early drives the fast price discovery
The stock price should be unaffected until the next earnings release

questions.explanation: The point of the example is that informed investors' self-interest drives FAST price adjustment — (c) contradicts semi-strong EMH, and (e) is trivially false (material new info moves prices immediately, not at the next earnings release). (a) is false — fast price adjustment is the point of the EMH example. (b) is false — material news moves prices immediately.

questions.question: Under which EMH form(s) is technical analysis STRICTLY PREDICTED to fail at producing excess returns?

options.text: Weak form
Semi-strong form
Strong form
None — EMH says nothing about technical analysis
Only if commission costs are zero

questions.explanation: Technical analysis uses only historical price/volume, which is already reflected under weak form — so all three forms predict its failure. (d) and (e) are distractors.

questions.question: Which of the following are typically cited as core ASSUMPTIONS behind the Efficient Markets Hypothesis?

options.text: All market participants must have IDENTICAL information and beliefs for EMH to hold
Zero transaction costs and zero taxes are required assumptions for EMH
Prices adjust quickly to new information
All investors have identical information and identical beliefs
There are no transaction costs or taxes

questions.explanation: EMH does not require (d) — heterogeneous beliefs are central to generating trades. It also does not require (e) — frictionless markets are a separate idealization, not a prerequisite for EMH. (a) is false — EMH does not require identical beliefs. (b) is false — these are separate idealizations.

questions.question: Consider a portfolio manager claiming a Sharpe ratio of 5.0 on a 3-year track record. Given what EMH predicts, which interpretations are reasonable?

options.text: Such a Sharpe would attract competition that compresses future returns — a key EMH prediction
Survivorship bias — we are observing only the lucky survivor from a larger population of failed managers
Unreported leverage or hidden tail risk inflating the apparent Sharpe
Backtest overfitting — the track record is in-sample or the strategy was selected after the fact
Confirmation of strong-form EMH

questions.explanation: A Sharpe of 5 over 3 years is suspiciously high and suggests one of (a)–(d). It is not confirmation of EMH — quite the opposite: if EMH held, such returns would not persist. (a) is wrong — Sharpe 5 over 3 years is extremely rare and warrants scrutiny.

questions.question: Which of the following sources of information would require STRONG-form EMH to be inefficient for a trader to profit from?

options.text: Tomorrow's earnings announcement, leaked by a board member
An internal strategic plan not yet made public
Yesterday's closing price
The company's filed 10-K annual report
An announced merger already reported on Bloomberg

questions.explanation: Strong-form EMH requires even PRIVATE/insider information to be impounded in prices. (a) and (b) are non-public; (c), (d), (e) are public and are covered by semi-strong EMH.

questions.question: Grinold's Fundamental Law of Active Management states IR = IC × √BR. Which statements are correct?

options.text: IR always equals the Sharpe ratio of the portfolio's total returns, regardless of benchmark
IC (Information Coefficient) is the correlation between forecasted and realized excess returns
BR is a measure of AUM in dollars, not the number of forecasts
Performance scales linearly with breadth, not with its square root
IC can range from −1 to +1

questions.explanation: Performance scales with √BR, not BR — doubling breadth multiplies IR by √2, not 2. This is the core insight of the law. (a) is wrong — IR uses alpha (excess over benchmark), not total return. Sharpe uses total excess over risk-free. (c) is false — breadth counts independent forecasts per year, not capital.

questions.question: Manager A has IC = 0.10 and makes 10 forecasts per year. Manager B has IC = 0.02 and makes 1,000 forecasts per year. Using the Fundamental Law, which statements are correct?

options.text: Manager A's IR equals her IC times BR (not √BR): 0.10 × 10 = 1.0
Manager B's IR = 0.02 × 1000 = 20
Manager B has higher IR despite much weaker per-forecast skill
Manager A has higher IR because IC is larger
The two managers have identical IR because skill × breadth is a linear tradeoff

questions.explanation: Calculations: A → 0.10 × √10 ≈ 0.316; B → 0.02 × √1000 ≈ 0.632. B has higher IR. The tradeoff is with √BR, not linear BR. (a) is false — the formula uses √BR, not BR. (b) is false — √1000 ≈ 31.6, not 1000.

questions.question: Warren Buffett (high IC, low breadth) and Jim Simons' Renaissance (low IC per trade, massive breadth) can achieve similar performance. Which statements correctly apply the Fundamental Law?

options.text: The Fundamental Law predicts that skill (IC) scales linearly with breadth — doubling BR doubles required IC
The √ scaling means Simons needs breadth to increase quadratically to compensate for linearly smaller IC
Doubling breadth only requires a linear decrease in IC to compensate
Buffett's strategy is demonstrably superior because high IC always beats low IC
Infinite breadth would allow arbitrarily low IC to produce arbitrarily high IR, ignoring real-world constraints

questions.explanation: (d) is false — the law says the two strategies are equivalent if the arithmetic works out. (e) is TRUE in the mathematical abstraction but breaks down due to liquidity limits, execution costs, and correlation between forecasts. (a) is wrong — the scaling is √BR, so doubling BR requires IC × √2 ≈ 1.41× more, not 2×. (c) is false — the scaling is √BR, so doubling BR needs IC × √2 ≈ 1.41, not 2×.

questions.question: Regarding the Information Coefficient (IC), which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Real-world IC values are typically in the 0.02 to 0.15 range for skilled managers
IC = +1 means perfect positive correlation between forecast and realized return
IC = −1 means the manager is systematically wrong — one could profit by inverting every forecast
Real-world IC values are typically in the 0.02 to 0.15 range for skilled managers
IC of 0.5 is routinely achieved by professional managers

questions.explanation: Real-world ICs above 0.1–0.2 are exceedingly rare. An IC of 0.5 would be extraordinary and unsustainable. (a) is wrong — real-world IC is typically 0.02–0.15; values >0.5 are unheard of.

questions.question: The Fundamental Law implicitly assumes forecasts are INDEPENDENT. Which of the following violate this assumption and therefore complicate the law's direct application?

options.text: Betting on 500 stocks that are all highly correlated within the same sector
Placing the same directional bet on the same stock 1000 times per day via a high-frequency strategy
Placing 500 truly independent bets on uncorrelated factors INCREASES breadth legitimately
A single bet scaled into using a ladder of limit orders
Betting on 500 low-correlation assets across asset classes INCREASES independence

questions.explanation: (a), (b), and (d) are all effectively the same bet repeated. The law requires independent breadth; redundant forecasts do not add to BR. (c) and (e) maintain independence and appropriately add to BR. (c) is a TRUE breadth scenario — but the question asked about VIOLATIONS. Reclassify: this doesn't violate independence. (e) is a TRUE breadth scenario, not a violation.

questions.question: Which of the following are correct distinctions between the Information Ratio and the Sharpe Ratio?

options.text: IR and Sharpe are identical in every setting; they are just different names for the same formula
IR uses tracking error in the denominator; Sharpe uses total volatility
IR is used to measure transaction-cost efficiency, not skill
Sharpe can be computed for any portfolio; IR requires a specified benchmark
IR and Sharpe are mathematically identical for any portfolio

questions.explanation: IR and Sharpe coincide only in the edge case where the benchmark is the risk-free rate (and tracking error equals total vol). In general they differ meaningfully — (e) is false. (a) is wrong — they differ: IR uses alpha/tracking-error; Sharpe uses excess-return/total-vol. (c) is false — IR measures active-management skill (risk-adjusted alpha).

questions.question: A fund manager claims that doubling AUM (assets under management) will double IR because more capital lets her trade more signals. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: AUM is not the same as breadth — more capital does not create new independent forecasts
Doubling AUM typically increases market impact, which degrades execution and lowers realized IC
Larger positions force the manager into less liquid names or larger trade sizes that reduce effective IC
The manager's claim correctly applies the Fundamental Law
Most alpha strategies have a capacity limit beyond which IR actually declines with more AUM

questions.explanation: (d) is false — the manager confuses CAPITAL with BREADTH. More capital can even REDUCE IR because of capacity constraints. (a) is wrong — AUM does not create breadth, and more capital typically DEGRADES IC via market impact.

questions.question: Consider a two-asset portfolio with weights w_A and w_B (w_A + w_B = 1). Which formula correctly gives portfolio variance?

options.text: σ_P² = w_A² · σ_A² + w_B² · σ_B² WITHOUT any covariance term
σ_P² = w_A · σ_A² + w_B · σ_B² (weighted average of individual variances)
σ_P² equals the weighted average of individual variances when ρ_{AB} = 0
σ_P² = (w_A · σ_A + w_B · σ_B)² always
Cross-terms (involving ρ_{AB}) can make σ_P LESS than either σ_A or σ_B alone

questions.explanation: Variance is NOT the weighted average of variances (b). Even when ρ = 0, cross-terms vanish but the formula still has squared weights in front, not linear ones — so (c) is false unless the cross-terms specifically cancel. (a), (d), (e) capture Markowitz's insight. (a) is false — the cross-covariance term cannot be omitted. (d) is false — this assumes perfect positive correlation only.

questions.question: Markowitz's insight is that portfolio risk depends on covariance, not just individual asset volatilities. Which of the following correctly illustrate the insight?

options.text: Diversification is impossible when all assets have positive expected returns
Two stocks with high individual volatility but low correlation may form a lower-volatility portfolio than a single 'safe' bond
The weighted average of expected returns is generally LESS than the portfolio's expected return
Diversification benefit is maximized with assets that have perfect negative correlation (ρ = −1)
Portfolios of perfectly correlated assets (ρ = 1) offer no diversification benefit on risk

questions.explanation: Expected portfolio return IS the weighted average — (c) is false. Variance reduction is the diversification benefit, not return reduction. The other statements are standard MVO results. (a) is wrong — diversification is about VARIANCE reduction via covariance, unrelated to return signs. (c) is false — weighted average EQUALS the portfolio's expected return.

questions.question: The efficient frontier is plotted as expected return vs. volatility. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The efficient frontier's upper curve is the set of portfolios offering maximum return for a given level of risk
The frontier's lower curve (if plotted) represents DOMINATED portfolios — same risk for lower return
Any portfolio strictly inside the frontier is suboptimal
The frontier is globally static and does not change with new return/risk estimates
A tangent line from the risk-free rate to the frontier identifies the maximum-Sharpe portfolio

questions.explanation: (d) is false — the frontier shifts whenever inputs (expected returns, volatilities, covariances) are re-estimated, which is a major practical challenge of MVO. (a) is wrong — the frontier is CURVED (hyperbolic in (σ, E[r]) space) due to the square-root relationship with variance.

questions.question: Mean-Variance Optimization (MVO) takes expected returns, a covariance matrix, and a target return, and outputs optimal weights. Which statements about MVO in practice are TRUE?

options.text: MVO is robust to small perturbations in expected-return estimates
Estimated covariance matrices degrade in accuracy as the number of assets grows relative to the sample size
Classical MVO performs consistently well out-of-sample because estimation errors are small
Adding constraints (e.g., no short-selling, max weight per asset) tends to produce more stable, realistic portfolios
MVO guarantees out-of-sample outperformance relative to naive equal-weight portfolios

questions.explanation: (e) is false — the DeMiguel et al. (2009) result famously showed that 1/N (equal-weight) often beats optimized MVO out of sample due to estimation error. MVO is optimal IN-SAMPLE but fragile OUT-OF-SAMPLE. (a) is wrong — MVO is NOTORIOUSLY sensitive to input perturbations. (c) is false — MVO is famously sensitive to estimation errors (DeMiguel et al.).

questions.question: Consider three assets: ABC (σ = 15%), DEF (σ = 15%, ρ with ABC = +0.9), GHI (σ = 15%, ρ with ABC = −0.9). Which of the following 50/50 pairs produces the lowest portfolio volatility?

options.text: 50% ABC + 50% DEF
50% ABC + 50% GHI
The two pairs produce identical portfolio volatilities because the assets have equal individual volatility
Pair (b) because ρ = −0.9 maximizes diversification
The choice depends on expected returns, not covariance

questions.explanation: Volatility only depends on weights, vols, and correlations — not on expected returns. With ρ = −0.9, pair (b) has dramatically lower σ_P than pair (a) which has ρ = +0.9.

questions.question: The maximum-Sharpe portfolio (tangency portfolio) lies at the tangent between a line from the risk-free rate and the efficient frontier. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: The tangency portfolio has the LOWEST Sharpe ratio among feasible portfolios
Under CAPM, the tangency portfolio is the RISK-FREE asset itself
Combining the tangency portfolio with the risk-free asset traces the Capital Market Line (CML)
Every point on the CML dominates the corresponding point (same risk) on the efficient frontier
The tangency portfolio is always the minimum-variance portfolio

questions.explanation: The tangency and min-variance portfolios are typically DIFFERENT points on the frontier. Min-variance lies at the leftmost tip; tangency lies further up-right where the tangent line touches. (a) is false — it has the HIGHEST Sharpe. (b) is false — under CAPM the tangency portfolio is the MARKET portfolio.

questions.question: The two-fund separation theorem states that every efficient portfolio can be constructed as a combination of the risk-free asset and the tangency portfolio. Which implications are correct?

options.text: All investors must hold different risky portfolios depending on their risk preferences
Risk-free lending/borrowing at a common rate is NOT required for the theorem
More risk-averse investors lend at the risk-free rate; less risk-averse investors borrow to leverage into the tangency portfolio
This theorem requires that short-selling be disallowed
It is a building block of the Capital Asset Pricing Model

questions.explanation: The two-fund theorem actually REQUIRES the ability to take positive and negative positions, and borrowing/lending at the risk-free rate — (d) is wrong. (a) is false — two-fund separation says all hold the same risky portfolio. (b) is false — it IS required for the theorem to hold.

questions.question: Which of the following are practical limitations of classical MVO?

options.text: MVO always models fat tails and skewness correctly
Treats volatility as the only risk measure — ignores downside risk and skewness
MVO properly captures higher-moment risks like skewness and kurtosis
Assumes a static one-period horizon — ignores dynamic portfolio decisions
Performs beautifully in practice because estimation errors are small

questions.explanation: Estimation errors are in fact LARGE, especially for expected returns — famously, 'errors in inputs of 10% can produce errors in outputs of 100%' (Michaud, 1989). (e) is the opposite of reality. (a) is wrong — classical MVO assumes normality and ignores higher moments. (c) is false — classical MVO ignores higher moments.

questions.question: A market simulator processes a list of orders into a portfolio value time series. Which of the following are CORE input components?

options.text: An orders file specifying only the Symbol but no Date or Quantity
Starting cash balance
Commission costs must be negligible to run a valid simulator
Market-impact cost (e.g., 0.5% of trade value)
The true future realized returns of each stock

questions.explanation: A simulator uses historical prices — it does not need 'future returns' as inputs. Inputs are orders, starting cash, and cost parameters. (a) is wrong — a valid orders file must include Date, Symbol, Action, and Quantity. (c) is false — commissions should be INCLUDED to model realism.

questions.question: The standard vectorized market-simulator approach uses four DataFrames. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Prices DataFrame: must exclude dividend-paying stocks to avoid confusion
Trades: the daily change in share holdings per symbol (only non-zero on days with orders)
Holdings: cumulative sum of the Trades DataFrame — the portfolio composition at end-of-day
Values: element-wise product of Holdings and Prices, summed across columns to get daily portfolio value
Cash column in Prices varies over time based on interest rates

questions.explanation: The cash column in Prices is a constant 1.0 — cash does not appreciate in the basic simulator. Interest-bearing cash can be modeled separately but is not the default. (a) is wrong — Prices includes all tradeable symbols (dividend-paying or not) with adjusted close.

questions.question: Which statements about commission and market impact in a backtest are TRUE?

options.text: Commission applies to BOTH buys and sells — cash is reduced on each side
Market impact is typically modeled as a percentage of the trade's dollar value
For buys, impact makes the effective price higher than the quoted price
For sells, impact makes the effective proceeds lower than the quoted price
Ignoring commission and impact in backtests is safe because they cancel out over many trades

questions.explanation: Ignoring frictions is a common and dangerous backtesting error — they compound strictly unfavorably and can turn a profitable-looking strategy negative. (a) is wrong — commissions apply to both sides of a trade.

questions.question: Consider a strategy that shows a 15% annual return in a zero-cost backtest but a −2% annual return once realistic frictions are applied. Which interpretations are sensible?

options.text: The strategy is actually MORE profitable once frictions are applied because they reduce taxes
The edge per trade is smaller than the round-trip cost
Market impact improves with higher turnover
The frictions are cosmetic and can be safely ignored for paper trading
A reasonable next step is to add transaction costs to the training objective or the reward function

questions.explanation: (d) is absolutely wrong — the frictions indicate the strategy is not economically viable. Paper trading without realistic costs will produce optimistic estimates that do not survive in live execution. (a) is wrong — transaction costs never improve profitability. (c) is false — impact gets worse with larger, faster trading.

questions.question: Leverage emerges in a market simulator when certain conditions hold. Which conditions indicate leveraged positions?

options.text: Cash balance remaining positive always implies leverage
Leverage is defined solely by number of positions held
The portfolio holds short positions (negative share counts)
The portfolio holds any positions at all
Total portfolio value is negative

questions.explanation: (d) is trivially true (holding any position is not leverage by itself). (e) indicates insolvency, not leverage — leverage can exist well before negative equity. (a) is false — positive cash implies no borrowing. (b) is false — leverage depends on gross vs. net exposure, not count.

questions.question: You notice that a vectorized simulator produces different results than a naive loop-based simulator for the same orders. What are plausible causes?

options.text: Vectorized code produces bit-identical results to loops in all cases — discrepancies indicate sabotage
The vectorized version computes holdings via cumsum, but the loop version has an off-by-one error
Loops and vectorized code must differ on ALL orders, otherwise one is broken
Float-point rounding differs between a Python loop (Python floats) and NumPy vectorization
The vectorized approach cannot handle multiple orders on the same day correctly

questions.explanation: (e) is false — vectorized code aggregates same-day orders via group-by or sum operations, which is actually cleaner than looping. The real issues are usually off-by-one indexing or date-alignment bugs. (a) is wrong — floating-point differences and subtle indexing bugs commonly cause small discrepancies. (c) is false — they should match on correct implementations; differences indicate bugs.

questions.question: Which performance metrics are typically computed from a market simulator's output time series?

options.text: Portfolio volatility measured on data AFTER the backtest ends
Daily return: (value_t / value_{t-1}) − 1
Sharpe ratio is computed without annualization
Maximum drawdown: the largest peak-to-trough decline
Final volatility measured over the FUTURE period (after the backtest ends)

questions.explanation: Metrics are computed over the backtest period, not future periods. (e) is a category error. (a) is wrong — metrics are computed from the backtest output, not future data. (c) is false — Sharpe is typically annualized via √252 for daily data.

questions.question: Bollinger Bands are constructed from a moving average and standard deviation. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Upper band = SMA_n + 2·σ_n
Lower band = SMA_n − 2 · σ_n
BB% = (Price − Lower) / (Upper − Lower)
A price touching the upper band is traditionally interpreted as overbought
Bollinger Bands guarantee a reversal whenever price breaches them

questions.explanation: No technical indicator GUARANTEES a reversal — (e) is false. Breaches can continue for extended periods. BBs identify tendencies, not certainties. (a) is wrong — upper and lower are swapped.

questions.question: The Relative Strength Index (RSI) is computed from average gains and losses. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: RS = average gain / average loss
RSI > 70 is traditionally labeled overbought; RSI < 30 is oversold
When average loss = 0, RS is undefined — implementations typically set RSI = 100 in that case
RSI is a trend-following indicator, not a mean-reverting one

questions.explanation: RSI is a mean-reversion (oscillator) indicator, not trend-following. It was designed by Wilder to identify extremes likely to reverse. (a) is wrong — RS is average gain over average loss, in that order.

questions.question: You are evaluating a trading strategy. Which of the following are backtesting PITFALLS that can produce inflated performance metrics?

options.text: Using random k-fold cross-validation on time-series data
Including stocks that have survived to the present day in historical backtests (survivor bias)
Repeatedly tweaking hyperparameters on the same test period
Ensuring training data strictly PRECEDES test data in time
Computing a state feature using the same-day close to make a trading decision that executes at that close

questions.explanation: Point-in-time data is the CORRECT practice, not a pitfall. The others — random k-fold (violates causality), survivor bias (~13% inflation), iterative tweaking (implicit overfitting), and same-close feature-trade (look-ahead bias) — all inflate backtest results. (d) is a BEST practice, not a pitfall. Pitfalls inflate results; best practices reduce inflation.

questions.question: The cumsum trick replaces a naive rolling-sum loop with a single O(n) operation. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: RollingSum_t(n) = CumSum_{t-n} − CumSum_t (subtract in reverse)
This eliminates an inner loop over the window, yielding large speedups (often 1000×)
The cumsum trick is APPROXIMATE — it introduces rounding noise by design
It is subject to floating-point precision loss when the cumulative sum grows very large
It cannot be used to compute moving averages

questions.explanation: Moving average = rolling sum / n, so (e) is false. (d) is a real concern with long sums and many small additions, though usually negligible for financial-data scales. (a) is wrong — the correct form is CumSum_t − CumSum_{t-n}; reversing changes the sign. (c) is false — the cumsum trick is mathematically exact (modulo float precision).

questions.question: Survivor bias in equity backtests. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Using current index membership to test historical periods is the MOST rigorous approach because it guarantees high data quality
This bias typically inflates historical returns because failed companies (which would have hurt returns) are excluded
Survivor bias typically DEFLATES backtested returns because survivors have lower historical vol
Using historical point-in-time index membership eliminates this bias
Survivor bias is a minor concern easily dismissed

questions.explanation: Survivor bias is a MAJOR concern — 13% inflation is not minor. It is a primary reason naive backtests look better than they are. (a) is wrong — using current membership ON historical data IS the survivor-bias mistake. (c) is false — survivor bias INFLATES returns by excluding failed companies.

questions.question: Regarding time-series cross-validation, which of the following schemes are VALID?

options.text: Rolling (walk-forward) validation: train on days 1..N, test on N+1..N+K, slide the window
Expanding window: train on days 1..N, test on N+1..N+K; then train on 1..N+K, test on N+K+1..; etc.
Random k-fold on shuffled days
Leave-one-out by randomly shuffling individual days
Train on days 1..N and test on days 1..N (same dataset)

questions.explanation: (c) and (d) violate temporal causality by allowing future info to leak into training. (e) is in-sample testing, not cross-validation — it is guaranteed to overfit. Only (a) and (b) respect time ordering.

questions.question: A reported strategy shows a Sharpe ratio of 7 over 5 years of daily returns. Which statements are reasonable reactions?

options.text: A Sharpe of 7 would be historically unprecedented for a multi-year strategy
The strategy is almost certainly overfit, leveraging a backtesting flaw, or has hidden risks
Demand the author provide the orders file and methodology for an independent replication
Check whether survivor bias, look-ahead, or iterative tuning contaminated the backtest
Such a Sharpe is common for well-designed quantitative strategies

questions.explanation: Sharpe of 7 is astronomical — even Renaissance Medallion is rumored to be in the 2–4 range on net returns. (e) is deeply wrong.

questions.question: Suppose an indicator fires a trading signal at today's close. Which execution assumptions are REALISTIC?

options.text: Execute at tomorrow's open (realistic; next available price after close)
Execute at today's close (requires the trader to have known the signal before close — look-ahead)
Execute at the average of tomorrow's OHLC (realistic only if simulating VWAP-like executions)
Execute at the LOW of tomorrow (cherry-picking — no real trader gets the daily low)
Execute at the HIGH of tomorrow for sells (cherry-picking)

questions.explanation: (b) is look-ahead; (d) and (e) are bucket examples of cherry-picked fills that no live execution could achieve consistently. Tomorrow's open or volume-weighted realistic fills are the honest defaults.

questions.question: Regarding stock splits and adjusted close prices, which statements are correct?

options.text: A 2:1 split halves each subsequent share's price while doubling share count
For backtesting, historical prices before the split are retroactively divided by the split ratio so the time series is continuous
The unadjusted close on the day of a 2:1 split would appear to drop by 50% — a meaningless 'price change'
Multiple splits compound: a 4:1 followed later by a 2:1 effectively divides pre-first-split prices by 8
Adjusted close prices are INVARIANT across time — once computed, they never change

questions.explanation: (e) is false: adjusted close is PATH-DEPENDENT — as new splits/dividends occur, historical adjusted values shift. The same calendar date will have different adjusted close values depending on when you pull the data. (a) is wrong — 2:1 HALVES the price and DOUBLES the count.

questions.question: Dividend adjustments to historical prices. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Dividends have no impact on the stock price on the ex-dividend date
Adjusted close retroactively reduces pre-dividend prices by the proportional dividend amount
A $1 dividend on a $100 stock adjusts pre-dividend prices down by 10%
Ignoring dividend adjustments causes backtests to understate the true total return of dividend-paying stocks
Dividends are a form of investor loss because the share price drops

questions.explanation: Dividends are NOT a loss to investors — they are cash paid out. The share-price drop is offset by the cash received. Total return includes both price changes and dividends. (a) is wrong — the stock typically drops by approximately the dividend amount on ex-div date. (c) is false — the adjustment is proportional: $1/$100 = 1%, not 10%.

questions.question: A stock has the following sequence: 2020 4:1 split, 2022 2:1 split. When computing TODAY's adjusted close for a 2019 date, which multipliers apply?

options.text: Only the FIRST split affects 2019 prices; later splits are ignored
2019 prices are multiplied (not divided) by the cumulative factor
A 2019 price is divided by a cumulative factor of 8
A 2019 price is divided by 4 only — only the first split matters
A 2021 price is divided by 2 (only the post-first-split second split affects it)

questions.explanation: Splits compound backward in time. 2019 prices see both splits: ÷4 × ÷2 = ÷8. 2021 prices see only the 2022 split (÷2). (d) is wrong because it ignores the compounding. (a) is false — all splits compound backward through the pre-split history. (b) is false — you DIVIDE historical prices by cumulative split ratio.

questions.question: Tick data, OHLCV bars, and aggregation. Which statements are correct?

options.text: A tick is an aggregated OHLCV bar for one minute of trading
A daily OHLCV bar aggregates all ticks within that day into Open, High, Low, Close, and Volume
In OHLCV, the Close must always equal either the High or the Low of the session
Volume represents the number of trades executed, not the number of shares
Multiple exchanges may report different prices for the same stock at the same instant

questions.explanation: Volume is the total number of SHARES traded, not the number of trades. Otherwise the statements are standard. (a) is wrong — a tick is a SINGLE transaction; OHLCV is the aggregate. (c) is false — Close is the LAST trade price, which typically lies strictly between High and Low.

questions.question: When handling missing values in a price time series, which best practices apply?

options.text: Forward-fill missing days in the MIDDLE of a range using the last-known price
Backward-fill missing days at the BEGINNING using future prices is considered a lookahead-free technique
Backward-fill BEFORE forward-fill to ensure future prices are used first
Linear interpolation between two known prices is generally SAFER than forward-fill for equity prices
Simply dropping all rows with any NaN is usually acceptable because inner joins are robust

questions.explanation: Linear interpolation uses future information (the next known price) to fill current NaNs — this is look-ahead bias. Dropping rows via inner join can discard legitimate trading days where one stock had data but others didn't, distorting the analysis. (b) is false — using future prices is lookahead by definition; the correct use of bfill is for pre-IPO gaps where the 'future' is the first known price. (c) is false — the correct order is FORWARD FIRST, then backward, to avoid lookahead.

questions.question: Regarding activation functions in neural networks, which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Sigmoid: g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^{−z}); ranges 0 to 1
ReLU: g(z) = max(0, z); the modern default for hidden layers
Softmax: converts a vector of logits to a probability distribution; used in multi-class output layers
Sigmoid suffers from vanishing gradients for very large |z|
ReLU is strictly preferred over sigmoid because it is differentiable everywhere, including at z = 0

questions.explanation: (a)–(d) are standard correct statements. (e) is false in the specific claim: ReLU is NOT differentiable at z = 0 (it has a kink). In practice implementations just define the subgradient as 0 or 1 at that point, but it is a non-differentiable function strictly speaking. ReLU is preferred for other reasons (no saturation for z > 0, computational efficiency), not because of differentiability.

questions.question: A feed-forward neural network with a single hidden layer has the form f(X) = β_0 + Σ_k β_k · g(w_{k0} + Σ_j w_{kj} · X_j). Which statements about this architecture are correct?

options.text: The w terms are fixed hyperparameters chosen by the user before training
The β terms are the output-layer weights combining hidden activations linearly
g(·) must be linear for the network to be trainable with gradient descent
Without g(·), the model collapses to linear regression
Deep networks (many layers) with ReLU activation are strictly less expressive than a wide single-hidden-layer network

questions.explanation: (e) is false: deeper networks can represent some functions more EFFICIENTLY (fewer parameters) than wide shallow networks. Universal approximation says a single wide layer CAN approximate any function, but deep networks often do so with far fewer parameters. (a) is wrong — hidden-layer weights w are LEARNED from data, not fixed. (c) is false — linear g makes the whole network linear; nonlinearity is the point.

questions.question: Dropout is a regularization technique. Which statements about dropout are TRUE?

options.text: During training, each hidden unit is zeroed independently with probability p, per mini-batch
During training, each hidden unit's OUTPUT must be scaled by 1/(1−p) so expected activations match at test time (inverted dropout)
At test time, no units are dropped; the full network is used
Dropout approximates an ensemble average over many sub-networks
Dropout increases the risk of overfitting

questions.explanation: Dropout is a REGULARIZER — it DECREASES overfitting, not increases it. The other statements describe the standard algorithm correctly. (a) is wrong — dropout zeros units independently with probability p, not all at once.

questions.question: Regarding loss functions for neural networks, which statements are correct?

options.text: Squared-error loss is ideal for multi-class classification with probability outputs
Cross-entropy loss −Σ Σ y_{im} · log f_m(x_i) is standard for multi-class classification
Cross-entropy is equivalent to negative log-likelihood under a categorical output model
Cross-entropy pairs naturally with softmax output because the gradient simplifies nicely
Squared-error loss should be used for multi-class classification because it handles probabilities as numbers

questions.explanation: Squared-error on classification probabilities suffers from saturation (the gradient can vanish) and does not correspond to a principled probabilistic model. Cross-entropy is the standard choice. (a) is wrong — cross-entropy is the standard choice for classification; squared error suffers saturation.

questions.question: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are designed for image-like data. Which statements about CNN components are TRUE?

options.text: A convolutional layer applies one giant fully-connected filter to the entire image with no weight sharing
Weight sharing means the same filter is applied at every spatial location, drastically reducing parameter count
Pooling layers LEARN weights during training just like convolutional layers
Stride controls how far the filter moves per step; padding controls how the edges are handled
Deeper CNN layers typically detect simpler features (edges) while earlier layers detect object-level concepts

questions.explanation: The hierarchy is the REVERSE of (e): earlier layers detect simple features (edges, corners), deeper layers detect higher-level, object-like features. (a) is wrong — convolutional layers apply SMALL filters with weight sharing across spatial positions. (c) is false — max-pooling has no learnable parameters.

questions.question: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and their variants. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Vanilla RNNs process sequences fully in parallel, just like feed-forward networks
Vanilla RNNs suffer from vanishing and exploding gradients over long sequences
LSTMs always outperform GRUs regardless of task or data size
GRUs are a simplified variant of LSTMs with fewer gates
RNNs process sequences in parallel across time steps, like Transformers do

questions.explanation: RNNs are SEQUENTIAL by construction — they must process each time step before the next. This is a key limitation that Transformers remove via self-attention. (a) is wrong — RNNs are inherently sequential because h_t depends on h_{t-1}. (c) is false — LSTMs and GRUs have comparable performance on many tasks.

questions.question: Backpropagation through time (BPTT) is used to train RNNs. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: BPTT can backpropagate gradients through time without any of the vanishing/exploding problems
Gradients can vanish or explode exponentially with sequence length
Gradient clipping works by multiplying all gradients by 2.0 to amplify them
Truncated BPTT only backpropagates through a fixed recent window to limit compute
BPTT cannot handle sequences longer than the training batch size

questions.explanation: (e) is false: BPTT is independent of batch size. The per-sequence length determines how far gradients propagate back, not the batch size across parallel sequences. (a) is wrong — vanishing and exploding gradients are THE primary problems BPTT faces. (c) is false — gradient clipping REDUCES gradient magnitude when it exceeds a threshold.

questions.question: Consider training a neural network with stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Which statements about SGD and its variants are correct?

options.text: SGD always uses the entire training set for every parameter update
Momentum accelerates SGD by accumulating a moving average of past gradients
Adam adapts per-parameter learning rates using first and second moment estimates
A learning-rate schedule (decay over epochs) often improves convergence
Full-batch gradient descent always converges faster than SGD in practice for deep networks

questions.explanation: Full-batch GD is slower per step (more compute) and often gets stuck in sharp minima. SGD's noise actually helps escape saddle points and find flatter minima. (e) is false. (a) is wrong — SGD uses MINI-BATCHES; full-batch GD uses the entire set.

questions.question: The Universal Approximation Theorem states that a sufficiently wide feed-forward network with a single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function. Which statements about its implications are correct?

options.text: The Universal Approximation Theorem tells you exactly how to TRAIN the network to find the approximating weights
It specifies the number of hidden units required for any target function
It guarantees SGD can find the approximating weights in polynomial time
In practice, deeper networks often require FEWER total parameters than a single wide layer to approximate the same function
It implies deep learning is unnecessary in theory

questions.explanation: (e) is a common misinterpretation. The theorem is about representational capacity, not practical efficiency or trainability. Deep networks win on BOTH training ease AND parameter efficiency. (a) is wrong — it is an existence result, not a learnability result; training is a separate problem. (b) is false — the theorem is silent on the required width. (c) is false — learnability is not addressed.

questions.question: In a classification task with K classes, the softmax output layer computes f_m(x) = e^{Z_m} / Σ_ℓ e^{Z_ℓ}. Which properties hold?

options.text: Softmax outputs can be arbitrary real numbers outside [0, 1]
Softmax is invariant to SCALING logits by a positive constant
Softmax is a generalization of the logistic sigmoid to K > 2 classes
The softmax output is always one-hot (exactly one element equals 1)
Softmax is used with cross-entropy loss for multi-class classification

questions.explanation: Softmax outputs are CONTINUOUS probabilities in (0, 1); they are not one-hot. Only after argmax would you obtain a discrete class prediction. (a) is false — softmax outputs are strictly in (0, 1) and sum to 1. (b) is false — scaling logits DOES change the distribution (sharper or flatter). It is only invariant to SHIFTS.

questions.question: Regarding the Transformer architecture introduced in 'Attention Is All You Need' (2017), which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Self-attention forces each position to attend only to its immediate predecessor, just like an RNN
It removes the sequential bottleneck of RNNs, enabling massive parallelism during training
Transformers only work on image data, not text
Transformers require fewer parameters than equivalent RNNs for the same task
Attention weights capture dynamic relationships between tokens that depend on the input

questions.explanation: Transformers typically require MORE parameters than RNNs for similar capacity, not fewer — but their parallelism makes them far more efficient to train on modern hardware. (d) is false. (a) is wrong — self-attention attends to ALL positions in parallel, not just the predecessor. (c) is false — Transformers power LLMs, which are text-first models.

questions.question: An autoregressive LLM generates text by modeling P(w_n | w_1, ..., w_{n-1}). Which statements are correct?

options.text: Each token is sampled INDEPENDENTLY of all prior context, like a bag of words
The 'temperature' hyperparameter rescales logits before softmax; lower temperature makes sampling more deterministic
Temperature = 1.0 forces greedy decoding; temperature → 0 adds maximum randomness
Higher temperature increases diversity but also the risk of nonsensical or hallucinated output
LLMs maintain a structured knowledge database that they retrieve facts from

questions.explanation: (e) is a major misconception — LLMs are PROBABILISTIC text models, not fact databases. They generate statistically likely sequences and can produce fluent-sounding but factually incorrect text (hallucinations). (a) is wrong — autoregressive LLMs condition each token on ALL prior tokens. (c) is false — the relationship is inverted: T→0 is greedy, higher T is more random.

questions.question: Which of the following are core distinctions between discriminative and generative models?

options.text: Discriminative models learn the joint P(x, y); generative models learn only P(y|x)
Generative models learn P(x) or P(x, y) — the distribution of the data itself
A generative model can be used to SAMPLE new data points; a discriminative model typically cannot
Classification with logistic regression is a discriminative model; a Gaussian mixture model is generative
Generative models are strictly better than discriminative models for all prediction tasks

questions.explanation: For pure classification/prediction, discriminative models typically outperform generative ones because they directly target the quantity of interest. Generative models shine when the full data distribution is the goal (e.g., image synthesis, text generation). (a) is wrong — the roles are reversed. Discriminative: P(y|x). Generative: P(x) or P(x,y).

questions.question: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit 'hallucinations' — fluent but factually incorrect outputs. Which statements correctly describe WHY?

options.text: Hallucinations occur only when the training data itself contains explicit falsehoods
In regions of the text distribution with sparse training data, the model still emits statistically-likely (but unverified) tokens
LLMs contain an internal 'uncertainty meter' that flags when they are hallucinating
Higher temperature amplifies hallucination risk
Hallucinations are always caused by bugs in the inference code and can be eliminated with better engineering

questions.explanation: (e) is wrong — hallucinations are a FUNDAMENTAL consequence of the autoregressive likelihood-maximization objective. They cannot be eliminated by engineering alone; they require architectural or grounding changes (e.g., retrieval augmentation). (a) is wrong — hallucinations can arise in regions of sparse data even when training labels are accurate. (c) is false — LLMs have no such self-awareness mechanism by default.

questions.question: Consider applying an LLM in a finance workflow. Which of the following are REASONABLE applications, and which are dangerous misuses?

options.text: Relying on an LLM's free-text recommendation for trade execution WITHOUT any human or systematic risk controls is safe
Extracting sentiment from public news headlines — reasonable
An LLM's memorized numerical facts from pre-training are ALWAYS perfectly accurate
Relying on the LLM's memorized knowledge for precise historical financial figures (e.g., 'What was AAPL's revenue in Q3 2019?') — unreliable
Using an LLM to replace human risk management entirely — safe because LLMs are objective

questions.explanation: (e) is the opposite of best practice. LLMs can produce fluent but wrong content, have no legal accountability, and have well-documented biases. Human oversight is essential. (a) is wrong — LLMs can hallucinate; unsupervised trading on their output is dangerous. (c) is false — memorized facts can be outdated or incorrect; verification is needed.

questions.question: Which of the following are motivations and capabilities of self-attention in Transformers?

options.text: Self-attention requires tokens to be processed strictly one at a time, serially
Allows each token to 'attend to' the most relevant context tokens regardless of distance
Enables efficient parallel training on modern GPUs/TPUs
Naturally resolves ambiguity like 'bank' (river bank vs. financial institution) using surrounding context
