Completely eliminates the need for training data — Transformers generalize without supervision

questions.explanation: Transformers still require massive training data — typically more than RNNs — to reach their full capability. (e) is false. (a) is wrong — the key advantage is PARALLEL processing across positions.

questions.question: Which of the following are sources of algorithmic bias as classically categorized?

options.text: Historical bias means the training data was corrupted by a software bug
Representation bias: the training data under-represents certain groups
Measurement bias: the features/proxies used systematically mismeasure the target
Aggregation bias: a single model is applied to heterogeneous groups, masking subgroup differences
Latency bias: the model runs too slowly in production

questions.explanation: Latency is a systems/engineering concern, not a bias category. (a)–(d) are the canonical four sources in the Suresh & Guttag framework. (a) is wrong — historical bias means the WORLD that produced the data was itself biased, not a bug.

questions.question: The COMPAS recidivism prediction system and similar criminal-justice algorithms have been criticized for bias. Which statements accurately describe the issues?

options.text: Removing 'race' as an input feature fully eliminates racial bias in the model's predictions
False-positive rates were found to differ systematically across racial groups (equal opportunity violation)
Removing the protected attribute from the training data guarantees the model cannot learn bias
Removing 'race' as an explicit input variable eliminates bias
The issue demonstrates that algorithms can reproduce or amplify bias present in the historical data

questions.explanation: (d) is the fairness-through-unawareness fallacy — removing the protected attribute does NOT remove bias because other features (zip code, name, etc.) serve as proxies. (a) is wrong — this is the 'fairness through unawareness' fallacy. Correlated proxies remain. (c) is false — proxy features still encode the protected attribute.

questions.question: Distinguish between ALLOCATIVE and REPRESENTATIONAL harms. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Allocative and representational harms are mutually exclusive and never occur in the same system
Representational harm: the system reinforces stereotypes or symbolic subordination (e.g., image search for 'CEO' returning only men)
Allocative harms tend to be easier to quantify than representational harms
Both types can occur simultaneously in a single system
Representational harm is trivial and should not be regulated

questions.explanation: (e) is a normative claim that most researchers reject — representational harms can materially affect identity formation, public perception, and downstream opportunities. (a) is wrong — both can co-occur in the same system (e.g., a biased image search with downstream hiring effects).

questions.question: Feedback loops can AMPLIFY algorithmic bias over time. Which scenarios illustrate this?

options.text: Predictive-policing model sends more police to historically-over-policed areas → more arrests in those areas → data confirms the model's predictions → next iteration doubles down
A biased resume-screening model filters out more female applicants → future training data has fewer women → model becomes even more biased against women
A ONE-TIME deployment is immune to feedback loops because it runs only once
A model is deployed and its outputs are never used to inform further decisions, so biases cannot amplify
Feedback loops are only a concern in recommender systems and never in high-stakes domains like lending or justice

questions.explanation: (d) is a non-feedback-loop scenario — but (d)'s premise rarely holds in practice. (e) is false — feedback loops are especially concerning in high-stakes domains. (c) is false — feedback emerges over subsequent iterations; 'one-time' is rarely the case in production.

questions.question: Several fairness criteria exist, and Chouldechova's impossibility theorem shows they cannot all be simultaneously satisfied when base rates differ. Which of the following are fairness metrics?

options.text: Demographic parity requires equal accuracy across groups
Equal opportunity: P(ŷ=1 | A=0, Y=1) = P(ŷ=1 | A=1, Y=1) (equal TPR across groups)
Equalized odds is the requirement that accuracy equal 100% across all groups
Calibration: P(Y=1 | ŷ=p, A=a) = p for each group a
Minimum overall accuracy: the only metric that matters

questions.explanation: Accuracy is NOT a fairness metric — it says nothing about group-level disparities. The other four are established formal fairness criteria. (a) is wrong — demographic parity is about equal POSITIVE PREDICTION rates, not accuracy. (c) is false — equalized odds is about equal TPR AND equal FPR, not 100% accuracy.

questions.question: Lessons from the Therac-25 medical disaster are sometimes cited in algorithmic-bias discussions. Which takeaways apply broadly?

options.text: The Therac-25 lesson is that the machine-learning algorithm must always be blamed directly for any failure
Unit-testing the algorithm in isolation does not guarantee safety in deployment
User interface design and error-reporting matter as much as algorithmic correctness
Safety cases require considering how the system behaves under all foreseeable conditions, including unexpected inputs
Blaming individual operators is the most effective way to prevent future failures

questions.explanation: (e) is the 'bad apple' fallacy. Complex-system theorists (Reason, Rasmussen) emphasize that systemic factors — not individual error — are usually the root cause of catastrophic failures. (a) is wrong — the Therac-25 lesson is about SYSTEM-level failure, not blaming the algorithm alone.

questions.question: Exchange-traded stock options have standardized contract specifications. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: One option contract represents exactly 1 share of the underlying
A quoted option price of $2.73 means the contract costs $273 (price × 100)
American options can be exercised any time before expiration; European options only at expiration
The strike price is fixed at the time of contract writing
Option holders receive voting rights and dividends from the underlying stock

questions.explanation: Option holders do NOT receive dividends or voting rights — they merely have the RIGHT to buy/sell at the strike. (e) is false. (a) is wrong — the standard multiplier is 100 shares, not 1.

questions.question: For a long call option with strike K and premium P, which statements about P&L at expiration are correct?

options.text: Break-even at expiration for a long call: S = K − P (strike minus premium)
Maximum loss = P (the premium paid) — capped downside
Maximum gain = unlimited (as spot rises indefinitely)
If S < K at expiration, the option expires worthless and the loss = P
A long call is an obligation to purchase shares at expiration

questions.explanation: A long call is a RIGHT, not an obligation. The holder can let it expire worthless if OTM. (e) is false. (a) is wrong — break-even is K + P, not K − P.

questions.question: Time decay (theta) describes how an option's value erodes as expiration approaches. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Theta is STRICTLY LINEAR over time to expiration
For long option positions, theta is a headwind (position loses value as time passes, all else equal)
For short option positions, theta is a tailwind (the seller gains as value decays)
Theta is approximately ZERO for deep ITM options far from expiration
Theta is constant across all strikes and all times to expiration

questions.explanation: (e) is false — theta varies substantially with moneyness and time. It peaks near ATM as expiration approaches. Deep ITM options have minimal time value, so theta ≈ 0 there. (a) is wrong — theta is non-linear; decay accelerates near expiration.

questions.question: A covered call combines a long stock position with a short call at strike K. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: If stock rises above K, the shares are 'called away' — upside is capped at K plus the premium received
If stock stays below K, the call expires worthless — the investor keeps both the stock and the premium
The strategy profits from volatile upward moves beyond K far more than a simple buy-and-hold
It is a common income-generating strategy in flat-to-moderately-bullish markets
Downside risk is fully hedged by the covered call

questions.explanation: (c) is FALSE — the strategy caps upside, so large upward moves beyond K are worse for the covered-call writer than for a pure long position. (e) is false — the premium offsets only a small portion of potential downside; downside is NOT fully hedged.

questions.question: A standard (long) butterfly spread on calls involves buying 1 call at strike K_L, selling 2 calls at K_M, and buying 1 call at K_H, where K_L < K_M < K_H and the strikes are equally spaced. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Maximum profit of a long butterfly occurs when the stock price at expiration is either K_L or K_H
The butterfly profits from HIGH volatility pushing the stock far from K_M
Maximum loss is capped at the net premium paid
The payoff graph at expiration is tent-shaped, peaking at K_M
The butterfly has unlimited upside if the stock rises far above K_H

questions.explanation: (e) is false — the two long calls at K_L and K_H are exactly offset by the two short calls at K_M beyond K_H, making upside capped (payoff returns to zero above K_H). (a) is false — max profit is at K_M, not the wings. (b) is false — the butterfly profits from LOW volatility (stock settling near K_M).

questions.question: The Black-Scholes option pricing model. Which of the following are INPUTS to the formula?

options.text: The stock's EXPECTED RETURN μ is a required input to Black-Scholes
Strike price K
The strike price is not required — Black-Scholes computes it automatically
Risk-free interest rate r
Expected return on the underlying stock (μ)

questions.explanation: Notably, the EXPECTED RETURN (μ) is NOT an input to Black-Scholes — this is a key insight. Only volatility matters because the risk-neutral framework replaces μ with r. (a) is wrong — a key insight of Black-Scholes is that μ does NOT enter the formula; only volatility matters. (c) is false — strike K is a REQUIRED input.

questions.question: Implied volatility (IV) is the volatility that, when input to Black-Scholes, reproduces the market price of an option. Which statements about IV are correct?

options.text: Implied volatility is equal by construction to the historical realized volatility
IV typically varies across strikes, producing a 'volatility smile' or 'smirk'
The volatility smile is inconsistent with Black-Scholes' assumption of constant volatility
Higher IV means more expensive options, all else equal
IV is always equal to the historical realized volatility of the underlying

questions.explanation: IV is forward-looking (market's expectation); realized volatility is backward-looking. They typically differ, especially in stressed markets. (e) is false. (a) is wrong — IV and realized volatility typically DIFFER; IV is forward-looking.

questions.question: The Kamel interview discusses why Gaussian assumptions for returns are dangerously inaccurate. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Gaussian models OVERESTIMATE the probability of extreme events in financial markets
Jump-diffusion models mix two distributions: a 'normal' regime and a low-probability 'jump' regime with much larger variance
VaR calculated under a Gaussian assumption typically UNDERESTIMATES true tail risk
The 1987 Black Monday crash would have been a 20+ sigma event under a Gaussian model — essentially impossible
Historical data shows market returns are well-modeled by a simple Gaussian distribution in all time horizons

questions.explanation: (e) is completely false — empirical returns have excess kurtosis, volatility clustering, and skewness. Gaussian dramatically understates tail risk. (a) is wrong — Gaussian UNDER-estimates extremes because real returns have fat tails.

questions.question: Which of the following are insights from the Kamel interview about designing a quantitative data infrastructure at scale?

options.text: At billions of data points, traditional SQL databases are strictly faster than NoSQL solutions for numerical time-series workloads
NoSQL stores always provide strict ACID guarantees for financial transactions
Point-in-time data and revised data produce identical backtests by construction
Revised (restated) data is ideal for backtesting because it is more accurate than the original
Multiple competing vendors help detect errors faster than a single monopoly data source

questions.explanation: (d) is the opposite of truth — restated data introduces look-ahead bias because it shows values that weren't known at the historical date. PIT data is the gold standard for backtesting. (a) is wrong — traditional SQL becomes a bottleneck at such scale; specialized stores are typically faster. (b) is false — most NoSQL stores relax ACID in favor of scalability. (c) is false — they differ exactly because revisions introduce lookahead.

questions.question: The 'alpha lifecycle' describes how quantitative strategies decay over time. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Alpha strategies are permanent physical laws that never decay
Exploitation phase: other participants find the same anomaly and trade against it, compressing returns
Evaporation phase: returns shrink below cost or disappear entirely as competition saturates
Alpha strategies behave more like depreciating assets than permanent physics laws
A discovered alpha persists indefinitely as long as the code is not published

questions.explanation: (e) is false — alpha can decay without public disclosure, through regime changes, market-structure evolution, or other managers independently discovering similar edges. (a) is wrong — alpha strategies are depreciating assets, not permanent laws.

questions.question: Which of the following are warning signs of a strategy that may be OVERFIT rather than genuinely edge-producing?

options.text: Consistent performance across multiple unrelated markets and decades is a classic WARNING sign of overfitting
The strategy rule is highly complex with many parameters tuned on the same data
High in-sample Sharpe is irrelevant to overfitting risk
The economic rationale is unclear — 'it just works'
The strategy performs consistently across multiple unrelated markets and decades

questions.explanation: (e) is a GOOD sign (robustness), not a warning sign. Overfit strategies fail to generalize across markets and time periods. (a) is wrong — such consistency is a sign of ROBUSTNESS, not overfitting. (c) is false — high in-sample + low out-of-sample is a CLASSIC overfitting signal.

questions.question: Why have classical statistical arbitrage and yield-curve arbitrage strategies lost much of their profitability since the 1990s?

options.text: Statistical arbitrage has been specifically outlawed by financial regulators since 2000
Retail day-traders continue to outnumber institutional algorithms in equities
Crowding has DECREASED since the 1990s as fewer firms run quantitative strategies
Regulation has outright banned statistical arbitrage strategies
Easy anomalies have been priced in; modern alpha requires exotic data and multi-factor combinations

questions.explanation: Statistical arbitrage is legal; there is no ban. The decline is driven by competition, regime change, market-structure evolution, and the exhaustion of simple anomalies. (a) is wrong — stat arb is legal; its decline is due to crowding and regime change, not regulation. (b) is false — institutional algos now dominate volume. (c) is false — crowding has INCREASED dramatically.

questions.question: Good strategy-design principles emphasized by practitioners include which of the following?

options.text: Strategy simplicity is a weakness; the most complex rules always perform best out-of-sample
Simplicity: fewer parameters and simpler rules generalize better
Out-of-sample testing on truly unseen data is considered excessive and unnecessary
Black-box neural networks with no explainability are preferred because they discover everything automatically
Realistic transaction costs must be included in the backtest from the start

questions.explanation: Unexplainable black boxes are a risk-management nightmare — they can fail silently in new regimes and provide no diagnosis path. (d) is the opposite of best practice. (a) is wrong — simplicity generalizes better; complexity is a common overfitting signal. (c) is false — OOS testing is essential best practice.

questions.question: ML for trade execution aims to minimize slippage and market impact. Which statements correctly define these concepts?

options.text: Slippage and market impact are exactly synonymous terms
Market impact: the price movement caused by the execution of a large order
Liquidity risk: the risk of not being able to execute at all at reasonable prices
Temporary impact: price movement that reverses after execution completes
Slippage and market impact are synonymous

questions.explanation: Slippage is the TOTAL realized cost; market impact is one COMPONENT of it (alongside spread, fees, timing risk). (e) is false. (a) is wrong — slippage is the total realized cost; market impact is one component of it.

questions.question: Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP) and Time-Weighted Average Price (TWAP) are common execution benchmarks. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: VWAP weights price by TIME intervals equally, while TWAP weights by VOLUME
A VWAP execution algorithm slices an order proportionally to historical volume profiles
TWAP is simpler but may under-execute during high-volume periods and over-execute during low-volume ones
Executing a large order at VWAP usually produces LESS market impact than executing it all at open
TWAP is always superior to VWAP because it does not require volume forecasts

questions.explanation: (e) is too strong. TWAP is robust to volume-forecast errors but gives up the known advantage of tracking real market liquidity. Neither is universally superior. (a) is wrong — the definitions are SWAPPED. VWAP weights by volume; TWAP weights by time.

questions.question: Reinforcement learning has been applied to trade execution. Which problem features make RL a good fit?

options.text: Execution is a ONE-SHOT static decision with no temporal structure or feedback
A clear feedback signal: slippage (reward or cost) is measurable per execution
An adaptive policy can respond to changing order-book conditions in real time
Training data is plentiful: historical executions provide many episodes
Execution is a one-shot decision with no temporal structure

questions.explanation: Execution is INHERENTLY sequential — (e) is the opposite of the problem's structure. That's precisely why RL is natural here. (a) is wrong — execution is inherently SEQUENTIAL with feedback, which is why RL fits.

questions.question: A portfolio manager runs a strategy with 20 bps of predictive edge per trade. Which of the following are plausible concerns about its executability?

options.text: Transaction costs are always exactly zero for professional quantitative trading firms
Strategy capacity is inversely related to trade size — small funds may exploit it while large funds cannot
Market impact grows non-linearly (often roughly square-root) with trade size
Adverse-selection costs can erode edge as sophisticated counterparties trade against mispriced orders
Execution costs are essentially zero for liquid large-cap equities, so edge is preserved

questions.explanation: Even liquid large-caps have non-zero bid-ask spreads, market impact for large orders, and fees. (e) is false. (a) is wrong — even the best firms face non-zero spreads, impact, and fees.

questions.question: Which statements correctly distinguish temporary and permanent market impact?

options.text: Splitting a large order over time INCREASES temporary impact relative to executing all at once
Temporary impact PERSISTS indefinitely after execution completes
Permanent impact is entirely due to trader error rather than information content
Permanent impact is zero for pure liquidity-motivated (non-informational) trades
Splitting a large order over time typically REDUCES temporary impact by letting liquidity refill between slices

questions.explanation: (d) overstates: even non-informational trades have SOME permanent footprint due to inventory effects on market-makers and the information content the market INFERS about the trade's motivation. (a) is wrong — splitting DECREASES temporary impact by allowing liquidity to refill. (b) is false — temporary impact, by definition, mean-reverts. (c) is false — permanent impact reflects information or inventory effects.

questions.question: The CFA Handbook chapters discuss accelerated computing for AI in investments. Which statements about GPU acceleration are TRUE?

options.text: GPUs deliver speedups purely for sequential algorithms, not for parallel ones
Typical speedups over CPU for deep-learning training are 10–100×
GPUs slow down matrix multiplications compared to CPUs
Faster inference enables real-time applications like automated execution and live risk monitoring
Switching to GPUs eliminates the need for data curation and feature engineering

questions.explanation: (e) is false — 'data-centric AI' emphasizes that data quality, not compute speed, often determines model quality. GPUs accelerate iteration but don't solve data problems. (a) is wrong — GPUs excel at PARALLEL linear-algebra operations, not sequential ones. (c) is false — GPUs accelerate matrix ops by 10–100×.

questions.question: Explainable AI (XAI) in investment management. Which statements are correct?

options.text: XAI techniques produce a single global explanation that is uniformly faithful for every prediction
Applying XAI tools is required by law in all jurisdictions worldwide
Global feature importance and local per-prediction explanations are the same thing
Applying XAI necessarily improves the raw predictive performance of the underlying model
Faithful XAI is particularly important for high-stakes decisions (lending, trading)

questions.explanation: (d) is false — XAI explains existing predictions; it does not retrain the model to be more accurate. Explainability and accuracy are orthogonal objectives. (a) is wrong — methods like SHAP/LIME produce LOCAL explanations per prediction, not a single global one. (b) is false — requirements vary by jurisdiction and industry. (c) is false — they answer different questions.

questions.question: Alternative data sources are increasingly used in quantitative investing. Which of the following are common alt-data categories?

options.text: Published quarterly earnings reports are the canonical example of ALTERNATIVE data
Credit-card transaction aggregates
Natural-language processing of earnings-call transcripts and news
Web-scraping product pricing and inventory data
Published quarterly earnings reports

questions.explanation: Published earnings are classic FUNDAMENTAL data, not 'alternative' data. The alt-data label specifically refers to non-traditional, often unstructured sources. (a) is wrong — earnings reports are traditional fundamental data; alt data refers to non-traditional sources.

questions.question: Model drift is a production-AI concern. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: A model deployed once can be trusted forever without any monitoring
Data drift: the distribution of input features shifts, even if the target relationship is stable
Financial markets are particularly susceptible to both forms of drift due to regime changes
Continuous monitoring of input distributions and prediction distributions helps detect drift early
A model deployed once can be trusted forever without re-validation

questions.explanation: (e) is the opposite of best practice. Financial-model decay is fast and well-documented; continuous monitoring and periodic retraining are essential for any long-running deployment. (a) is wrong — models decay over time and continuous monitoring is essential.
